idiom_name: new Proxy(target, handler) typed as ProxyHandler<T> + Reflect
implementation_notes: The runtime mechanism is JavaScript's Proxy/Reflect, so TypeScript's contribution is only typing: ProxyHandler<T> names the traps and new Proxy<T>(target, handler) is declared to return T, which is wrong the moment a trap changes the object's shape (microsoft/TypeScript#20846). Shape-changing proxies therefore need an explicit interface plus a cast, and trap parameters stay loosely typed (string | symbol, any) by design, so the compiler cannot check the forwarding logic either.
pitfalls: The declared return type is the target's type, so a proxy that adds, hides or converts members is a lie the compiler cannot see; declare the exposed interface and cast deliberately.
Trap signatures give no key-level type safety: prop is string | symbol and the get trap returns any, so shape errors surface only at run time.
Decorators and reflect-metadata are the compile-time alternative, but metadata does not travel through a proxy automatically, so a proxied class can lose its decorator metadata.

variants.name: typed pre-ES2015 accessor membrane
variants.idiom_name: Object.defineProperty accessors behind a declared interface
variants.implementation_notes: For legacy targets the membrane is built by redefining accessors on a wrapper and declaring that wrapper's interface explicitly, which is why TypeScript users see this variant mostly in polyfill code: the type system can describe the wrapper honestly because the wrapper is a real object with real accessors, but the runtime can only trap reads and writes of the keys that existed when the membrane was built.
pitfalls: Property addition and deletion are invisible, and the in operator, ownKeys and calls are not trappable, so the declared interface can silently under-describe the target.
The membrane holds bound methods, so this-binding and prototype changes on the target are not reflected in the view.
